etymology_text:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₁es-
Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésti
Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH-
Proto-Indo-European *-t
Proto-Indo-European *bʰúHt
Proto-Italic *ezom~*som
Archaic Latin 𐌄𐌔𐌏𐌌 (esom)
Old Latin esum
Latin sum
From Proto-Italic *ezom~*som, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁ésti (“be”) + *bʰúHt (“become”). From the latter of the two derive all the /f-/ forms of Latin sum (including fore), the separate verb fīō (“become”), and the verb-endings -bō (future) and -bam (past imperfect). Clipped conjugations with /s-/, such as sum itself, occurred alongside more conservative equivalents with /es-/ in early Latin, such as the archaic esum. The clipped forms likely arose as unstressed clitics.

From Proto-Italic *werðom, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰom (“word”). Cognate with Umbrian 𐌖𐌄𐌓𐌚𐌀𐌋𐌄 (uerfale), English word.

etymology_text: Perhaps inherited from Proto-Italic *amāō, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃emh₃- (“to take hold of”). Schrijver alternatively proposes that the term reflects an *ē-stative formed to a root present, adducing as evidence amor (“love”). Formations in -or are otherwise rare beside ā-verbs, but are common beside second conjugation stative verbs.

etymology_text:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₂ey-
Proto-Indo-European *-u
Proto-Indo-European *h₂óyu
Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-
Proto-Indo-European *-os
Proto-Indo-European *h₂yéwos
Proto-Italic *jowos
Archaic Latin *iowos, *iowez-
Proto-Indo-European *-tós
Proto-Italic *-tos
Archaic Latin -tus
Archaic Latin iovestos
Latin iūstus
By surface analysis, iūs + -tus. From Archaic Latin iovestos, from *iowez- (the oblique stem of *iowos, whence iūs) + -tos. Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂yew-.

examples.text: Sicut audio, judico: et judicium meum iustum est, quia non quaero voluntatem meam, sed voluntatem ejus qui misit me.

examples.text: Ea tum cura maxime intentos habebat Romanos, non ab ira tantum, quae in nullam unquam ciuitatem iustior fuit, quam quod urbs tam nobilis ac potens, sicut defectione sua traxerat aliquot populos, ita recepta inclinatura rursus animos uidebatur ad ueteris imperii respectum.
examples.ref: 27 BCE – 25 BCE, Titus Livius, Ab urbe condita 26.1
examples.english: This concern in particular troubled the mindful Romans at the time, not so much because of anger, which has never been more justified against any other city, rather because a city so noble and powerful, in the same way that it had attracted the support of a number of communities by its revolt, was thought would again turn attention back towards respect for the previous government once recaptured.
